units.text: ⟦0⟧1 Measuring Program Resource Use⟦1⟧ ¶⟦2⟧⟦3⟧
units.sourceHTML: 1 Measuring Program Resource Use ¶

units.text: The ⟦0⟧ command runs another program, then displays information about the resources used by that program, collected by the system while the program was running. You can select which information is reported and the format in which it is shown (see ⟦1⟧Setting the Output Format⟦2⟧), or have ⟦3⟧ save the information in a file instead of displaying it on the screen (see ⟦4⟧Redirecting Output⟦5⟧).
units.sourceHTML: The time command runs another program, then displays information about the resources used by that program, collected by the system while the program was running. You can select which information is reported and the format in which it is shown (see Setting the Output Format), or have time save the information in a file instead of displaying it on the screen (see Redirecting Output).

units.text: The resources that ⟦0⟧ can report on fall into the general categories of time, memory, and I/O and IPC calls. Some systems do not provide much information about program resource use; ⟦1⟧ reports unavailable information as zero values (see ⟦2⟧Accuracy⟦3⟧).
units.sourceHTML: The resources that time can report on fall into the general categories of time, memory, and I/O and IPC calls. Some systems do not provide much information about program resource use; time reports unavailable information as zero values (see Accuracy).

units.text: ⟦0⟧ runs the program ⟦1⟧, with any given arguments ⟦2⟧…. When ⟦3⟧ finishes, ⟦4⟧ displays information about resources used by ⟦5⟧.
units.sourceHTML: time runs the program command, with any given arguments arg…. When command finishes, time displays information about resources used by command.

units.sourceHTML: 1.2 The Format String ¶

units.text: The ⟦0⟧format string⟦1⟧ controls the contents of the ⟦2⟧ output. It consists of ⟦3⟧resource specifiers⟦4⟧ and ⟦5⟧escapes⟦6⟧, interspersed with plain text.

units.text: A backslash introduces an ⟦0⟧escape⟦1⟧, which is translated into a single printing character upon output. The valid escapes are listed below. An invalid escape is output as a question mark followed by a backslash.

units.text: A resource specifier consists of a percent sign followed by another character. An invalid resource specifier is output as a question mark followed by the invalid character. Use ‘⟦0⟧’ to output a literal percent sign.

units.text: Number of major, or I/O-requiring, page faults that occurred while the process was running. These are faults where the page has actually migrated out of primary memory.

units.text: ⟦0⟧1.2.5 Termination Status⟦1⟧ ¶⟦2⟧⟦3⟧
units.sourceHTML: 1.2.5 Termination Status ¶

units.text: The following are ⟦0⟧two-letter specifiers⟦1⟧:
units.sourceHTML: The following are two-letter specifiers:

units.text: Exit type: the text ‘⟦0⟧’ or ‘⟦1⟧’, depending on how the command terminated. ‘⟦2⟧’ means the program terminated with any exit code, not just a zero exit code.
units.sourceHTML: Exit type: the text ‘normal’ or ‘signalled’, depending on how the command terminated. ‘normal’ means the program terminated with any exit code, not just a zero exit code.

units.text: Numeric exit code ⟦0⟧if⟦1⟧ the command exited normally (i.e., not terminated by a signal). This value is similar to ‘⟦2⟧’ format specifier, except that unlike ‘⟦3⟧’, this will be ⟦4⟧empty⟦5⟧ if the program was terminated by a signal.
units.sourceHTML: Numeric exit code if the command exited normally (i.e., not terminated by a signal). This value is similar to ‘%x’ format specifier, except that unlike ‘%x’, this will be empty if the program was terminated by a signal.

units.text: Numeric signal code ⟦0⟧if⟦1⟧ the command was terminated by a signal (e.g., the value ‘⟦2⟧’ if the program was terminated by SIGKILL). Empty if the program exited normally (i.e., not terminated by a signal).
units.sourceHTML: Numeric signal code if the command was terminated by a signal (e.g., the value ‘9’ if the program was terminated by SIGKILL). Empty if the program exited normally (i.e., not terminated by a signal).

units.text: Signal name ⟦0⟧if⟦1⟧ the command was terminated by a signal (e.g., ‘⟦2⟧’ if the program was terminated by SIGKILL). Empty if the program exited normally (i.e., not terminated by a signal).
units.sourceHTML: Signal name if the command was terminated by a signal (e.g., ‘KILL’ if the program was terminated by SIGKILL). Empty if the program exited normally (i.e., not terminated by a signal).

units.text: The text ‘⟦0⟧’ ⟦1⟧if⟦2⟧ the command exited normally (i.e., not signalled) and with exit code zero. Empty otherwise.
units.sourceHTML: The text ‘ok’ if the command exited normally (i.e., not signalled) and with exit code zero. Empty otherwise.

units.text: ⟦0⟧1.3 Redirecting Output⟦1⟧ ¶⟦2⟧⟦3⟧
units.sourceHTML: 1.3 Redirecting Output ¶

units.text: By default, ⟦0⟧ writes the resource use statistics to the standard error stream. The options below make it write the statistics to a file instead. Doing this can be useful if the program you’re running writes to the standard error or you’re running ⟦1⟧ noninteractively or in the background.
units.sourceHTML: By default, time writes the resource use statistics to the standard error stream. The options below make it write the statistics to a file instead. Doing this can be useful if the program you’re running writes to the standard error or you’re running time noninteractively or in the background.

units.text: Write the resource use statistics to ⟦0⟧. By default, this ⟦1⟧overwrites⟦2⟧ the file, destroying the file’s previous contents.
units.sourceHTML: Write the resource use statistics to file. By default, this overwrites the file, destroying the file’s previous contents.

units.text: ⟦0⟧Append⟦1⟧ the resource use information to the output file instead of overwriting it. This option is only useful with the ‘⟦2⟧’ or ‘⟦3⟧’ option.
units.sourceHTML: Append the resource use information to the output file instead of overwriting it. This option is only useful with the ‘-o’ or ‘--output’ option.

1.5 Accuracy ¶

units.text: The elapsed time is not collected atomically with the execution of the program; as a result, in bizarre circumstances (if the ⟦0⟧ command gets stopped or swapped out in between when the program being timed exits and when ⟦1⟧ calculates how long it took to run), it could be much larger than the actual execution time.
units.sourceHTML: The elapsed time is not collected atomically with the execution of the program; as a result, in bizarre circumstances (if the time command gets stopped or swapped out in between when the program being timed exits and when time calculates how long it took to run), it could be much larger than the actual execution time.

units.text: When the running time of a command is very nearly zero, some values (e.g., the percentage of CPU used) may be reported as either zero (which is wrong) or a question mark.
units.sourceHTML: When the running time of a command is very nearly zero, some values (e.g., the percentage of CPU used) may be reported as either zero (which is wrong) or a question mark.

units.text: Most information shown by ⟦0⟧ is derived from the ⟦1⟧ system call. The numbers are only as good as those returned by ⟦2⟧. Many systems do not measure all of the resources that ⟦3⟧ can report on; those resources are reported as zero. The systems that measure most or all of the resources are based on 4.2 or 4.3BSD. Later BSD releases use different memory management code that measures fewer resources.
units.sourceHTML: Most information shown by time is derived from the getrusage system call. The numbers are only as good as those returned by getrusage. Many systems do not measure all of the resources that time can report on; those resources are reported as zero. The systems that measure most or all of the resources are based on 4.2 or 4.3BSD. Later BSD releases use different memory management code that measures fewer resources.

units.text: On systems that do not have a ⟦0⟧ call, the ⟦1⟧ system call is used instead. It provides much less information than ⟦2⟧, so on those systems ⟦3⟧ reports most of the resources as zero.
units.sourceHTML: On systems that do not have a getrusage call, the times system call is used instead. It provides much less information than getrusage, so on those systems time reports most of the resources as zero.

units.text: The ‘⟦0⟧’ and ‘⟦1⟧’ values are allegedly only “real” input and output and do not include those supplied by caching devices. The meaning of “real” I/O reported by ‘⟦2⟧’ and ‘⟦3⟧’ may be muddled for workstations, especially diskless ones.
units.sourceHTML: The ‘%I’ and ‘%O’ values are allegedly only “real” input and output and do not include those supplied by caching devices. The meaning of “real” I/O reported by ‘%I’ and ‘%O’ may be muddled for workstations, especially diskless ones.
